items.quote_a: **No Tolerable Upper Intake Level (UL) has been established** for chromium, due to insufficient long-term safety data. The FNB noted that caution may be warranted and that people with renal and liver disease might be susceptible to adverse effects from high intakes [2].
items.quote_b: **Chromium:** AI is 35 mcg for men 14-50 and 25 mcg for women 19-50. No UL has been established, but there are concerns about kidney damage at excessive intakes [15].
items.summary: A says only renal/liver-disease patients might be susceptible and that no adverse effects are definitively linked to high intakes, while B states a general concern about kidney damage at excessive intakes.
items.suggested_fix: Align the multivitamin text with the chromium reference: say people with renal or liver disease might be susceptible to adverse effects, and that kidney failure is only reported in case reports at high doses with causality not established.

items.quote_a: A typical cup (240 mL) of bone broth provides approximately 6-10 grams of protein, of which about 40-80% is collagen — yielding roughly 2.5-8 grams of collagen per cup [1][6].
items.quote_b: | Bone broth | 5-15 g per cup (varies widely) | Made by simmering animal bones; content varies by preparation time and source |
items.summary: The two excerpts give incompatible collagen content per cup of bone broth (about 2.5-8 g versus 5-15 g, and the upper figure exceeds the total protein per cup stated in A).
items.suggested_fix: Reconcile the per-cup collagen range between the two references. A's range is bounded by its stated 6-10 g protein per cup, so B's 5-15 g upper end looks too high unless a source supports it.

items.quote_a: To achieve the 10-15 grams of collagen per day used in most clinical trials for joint health, consider consuming 2-3 cups of bone broth daily [1].
items.quote_b: Hydrolyzed collagen for joint pain typically requires 5-10 grams daily.
items.summary: A says the joint-health trial dose is 10-15 g/day, while B gives 5-10 g/day for joint pain, so the target dose used to size bone broth intake differs.
items.suggested_fix: Align the joint-health collagen dose across both references. A's own table lists 5-10 g/day for exercise-related joint pain and 10-12 g/day for osteoarthritis, so the 10-15 g/day figure should be revised or qualified.

items.quote_a: Hydrolyzed collagen for joint pain typically requires 5-10 grams daily.
items.quote_b: **Hydrolyzed collagen peptides:** 5,000-12,500 mg/day
items.summary: The joint-health dose range for hydrolyzed collagen peptides is 5-10 g/day in one excerpt and 5-12.5 g/day in the other.
items.suggested_fix: Align the upper end of the hydrolyzed collagen joint dose in both references (10 g vs 12.5 g), or state which studies support the higher figure.

items.quote_a: | Joint pain (osteoarthritis) | UC-II (undenatured type II) | 40 mg (~10 mg collagen) | 3-6 months |
items.quote_b: - **Undenatured type II collagen (UC-II, NT2):** 40 mg/day (providing ~10 mg collagen), taken on an empty stomach at bedtime [1]
items.summary: The collagen reference gives a 3-6 month onset for UC-II joint benefit, while the joint-supplements reference advises stopping if there is no response by 3 months.
items.suggested_fix: Reconcile the expected time to benefit for joint supplements. Either note that collagen products may need up to 6 months, or soften the 3-month stop rule when it is applied to collagen.

items.quote_a: Lutein supplements are not known to have major drug interactions.
items.quote_b: Avoid taking vitamin A supplements with prescription medications in the retinoid family, as the combination increases the risk of toxicity and side effects.
items.summary: Not a clear contradiction: the two excerpts address different substances (lutein vs vitamin A), so no finding is warranted here.
items.suggested_fix: No change needed; the claims are about different supplements.

items.quote_a: No specific adverse effects were reported** in any of the three published clinical trials [1]
items.quote_b: Mild human adverse effects: headache, difficulty sleeping, flatulence, and gas [19].
items.summary: Excerpt A says no adverse effects were reported in any human trial, while excerpt B lists mild human adverse effects (headache, insomnia, flatulence, gas) for African mango.
items.suggested_fix: Reconcile the human adverse-effect statements. Either note the mild effects that B cites (headache, difficulty sleeping, flatulence, gas) in A, or clarify that B's source is not one of the three trials.

items.quote_a: While no liver toxicity has been reported with African mango, the absence of evidence is not evidence of absence, particularly given the limited safety monitoring in the available trials.
items.quote_b: One case of renal failure was associated with African mango in a patient with pre-existing chronic kidney disease [21].
items.summary: Excerpt B reports a case of renal failure associated with African mango in a CKD patient, while A's safety and special-population sections describe no reported serious harm and only advise caution in kidney disease.
items.suggested_fix: Mention the reported renal failure case in CKD in A's safety and special-population sections, and reconsider advising only 'use with caution' for kidney disease in light of it.

items.quote_a: Chia seeds' omega-3 fatty acid content (particularly ALA) may exhibit mild antiplatelet effects that could theoretically enhance the action of anticoagulant or antiplatelet medications, including [2][21]:
items.quote_b: **Chia seeds,** another ALA source, can modestly increase blood EPA levels (but not DHA) and have not been shown to improve risk factors for cardiovascular disease [16].
items.summary: A says chia's ALA content may raise EPA-related effects only theoretically on platelets, while B states chia raises blood EPA but does not improve cardiovascular risk factors, whereas A cites clinical trials showing blood pressure and triglyceride benefits at 25-30 g/day.
items.suggested_fix: Reconcile the chia cardiovascular evidence statements, either noting B's claim covers only specific trials or softening A's claim that trials show blood pressure and triglyceride effects.

items.quote_a: **For blood pressure and cardiometabolic support:** Clinical trials showing effects on blood pressure and triglycerides typically used 25–30 g per day [9][11].
items.quote_b: **Chia seeds,** another ALA source, can modestly increase blood EPA levels (but not DHA) and have not been shown to improve risk factors for cardiovascular disease [16].
items.summary: A reports clinical trials showing chia effects on blood pressure and triglycerides (cardiovascular risk factors), while B says chia has not been shown to improve cardiovascular risk factors.
items.suggested_fix: Align the evidence statements, clarifying which trials show effects on blood pressure and triglycerides and which evidence supports the claim of no demonstrated cardiovascular risk-factor improvement.

items.quote_a: Building bone in adolescent girls (ages 9-13):** 800 mg calcium with 400 IU vitamin D3 and 400 mg magnesium daily [32]
items.quote_b: The UL for supplemental magnesium (not including food sources) is **350 mg/day** for adults [1].
items.summary: The calcium page recommends 400 mg magnesium daily for girls aged 9-13, which exceeds the supplemental magnesium UL of 350 mg/day given on the magnesium page.
items.suggested_fix: Clarify whether the 400 mg magnesium refers to supplemental or total intake, or reconcile it with the 350 mg/day UL. Note that the UL as stated is for adults, so child-specific limits would need to be cited.

items.quote_a: Take medications at least 1 hour before or 2-4 hours after gel-forming fiber supplements [19][22].
items.quote_b: Take probiotics at least 2 hours apart from antibiotics [12].
items.summary: The prebiotics excerpt's own separation guidance is internally inconsistent, saying 2-4 hours after gel-forming fiber in one place and 'at least 1-2 hours' in another; this is not a conflict with the probiotics excerpt, which covers a different pairing (probiotics and antibiotics).
items.suggested_fix: This is a prebiotics-excerpt internal inconsistency, not a cross-excerpt conflict; reconcile the 2-4 hour and 1-2 hour separation statements within the prebiotics reference.

items.quote_a: Restless legs syndrome (ferritin <75 ng/mL):** 65 mg iron (from 325 mg ferrous sulfate) with 200 mg vitamin C, twice daily (Winkelman, Neurology 2016) [8].
items.quote_b: **For men, people with a history of kidney stones, or those with known defects in oxalate or vitamin C metabolism, it may be wise to limit supplemental vitamin C to RDA levels (75-90 mg) or no more than 250 mg per day [125].**
items.summary: A's restless-legs regimen pairs iron with 200 mg vitamin C twice daily (400 mg/day, a male-relevant dose above the 250 mg/day limit B suggests for men and stone-prone people) without any caveat.
items.suggested_fix: Note that the 400 mg/day vitamin C in the RLS regimen exceeds the 250 mg/day limit B suggests for men and people with kidney stone history, or cross-reference B's caution.

items.quote_a: **AREDS formula (AMD progression):** 500 mg/day as part of the AREDS combination supplement, recommended only for people with intermediate or advanced AMD in one eye [101][102].
items.quote_b: The Age-Related Eye Disease Study (AREDS), a landmark RCT, found that a combination supplement containing vitamin E (400 IU synthetic), beta-carotene, vitamin C (500 mg), zinc (80 mg), and copper (2 mg) reduced the risk of developing advanced AMD by 25% over 5 years in people already at high risk (intermediate AMD or advanced AMD in one eye) [43].
items.summary: Excerpt A restricts the AREDS formula to intermediate AMD or advanced AMD in one eye, while B describes the same population as at high risk, with advanced AMD in one eye as one qualifying group; the wording is inconsistent between the two.
items.suggested_fix: Align the eligibility description for AREDS in both articles. Note that the trial population was people at high risk (intermediate AMD or advanced AMD in one eye).

items.quote_a: Doses above 400 mg show diminishing returns in absorption. Too much can cause diarrhea and may increase cataract risk [15].
items.quote_b: Low-to-moderate doses (60-250 mg/day) may be protective rather than harmful (see Section 3).
items.summary: A links vitamin C excess generally to increased cataract risk, while B ties the increased risk to about 1,000 mg/day long-term (in women) and says low-to-moderate doses may be protective.
items.suggested_fix: Qualify the cataract statement in A to say the risk was seen with long-term intake around 1,000 mg/day, and that lower doses (60-250 mg/day) may be protective, as B describes.

items.quote_a: **Psyllium husk** (7g/day): 5–10% LDL reduction.
items.quote_b: Effective doses for cholesterol lowering range from 7-15 g/day, with greater effects at doses exceeding 10 g/day [12].
items.summary: The algorithm gives 7 g/day psyllium as the dose with a 5-10% LDL reduction, while the reference says greater effects need more than 10 g/day, with 7 g/day only the bottom of the range.
items.suggested_fix: Align the dose wording: either note that 7 g/day is the low end of the effective range and that more than 10 g/day gives greater effect, or state the 5-10% reduction for the 7-15 g/day range in both places.

items.quote_a: Glycine content, for example, can range from 500 to 1,700 mg per cup depending on preparation [5].
items.quote_b: | Bone broth | 100 g | 3–5 g (varies by preparation) |
items.summary: Glycine content of bone broth is given as 0.5-1.7 g per 240 mL cup in A but 3-5 g per 100 g (roughly 7-12 g per cup) in B, which cannot both be true.
items.suggested_fix: Reconcile the two glycine-content figures for bone broth against their sources and state them on a common serving basis. One of the two ranges is off by several-fold.

items.quote_a: The addition of 500 mg vitamin C did not enhance these effects [25].
items.quote_b: Vitamin C supplements at 250 mg or more can interfere with several diagnostic tests [6]:
items.summary: The collagen excerpt describes a skin study where adding 500 mg vitamin C gave no extra benefit, but the vitamin C excerpt treats 500 mg as a standard purpose-driven dose, which is a loose tension rather than a hard conflict.
items.suggested_fix: No change is clearly required; if kept, the collagen excerpt could note that the null result applies only to skin outcomes with collagen tripeptides.

items.quote_a: Research by Kumar et al. at Baylor College of Medicine has shown that GlyNAC supplementation in older adults and in people with HIV corrects age-related glutathione deficits and improves markers of oxidative stress, mitochondrial function, and inflammation.
items.quote_b: However, these studies have been small, conducted by the same research group, and lack rigorous placebo-controlled statistical comparisons.
items.summary: The glycine excerpt states GlyNAC research has shown it corrects glutathione deficits, while the NAC excerpt describes the same studies as small, single-group, uncontrolled and preliminary.
items.suggested_fix: Hedge the glycine excerpt's GlyNAC claim to match the NAC excerpt: the evidence is preliminary, from small studies by one research group without placebo controls.

items.quote_a: making it potentially more effective at raising glutathione levels than either amino acid alone [15].
items.quote_b: Whether GlyNAC is meaningfully superior to NAC alone at equivalent doses remains unestablished.
items.summary: The glycine excerpt implies GlyNAC is likely more effective than either amino acid alone, while the NAC excerpt says superiority over NAC alone is unestablished.
items.suggested_fix: Note in the glycine excerpt that superiority of GlyNAC over NAC alone has not been established.

items.quote_a: - **CKD (eGFR < 45):** `round(IBW * 1.0)` grams/day
items.quote_b: Brad's own daily target is 1.2 g of protein per kg of ideal body weight, and people with chronic kidney disease (stages 3 to 5) should consult their doctor about protein intake (Brad's current guidance, 31 Jul 2026).
items.summary: The algorithm cuts the protein multiplier to 1.0 g/kg IBW for eGFR < 45, while B gives 1.2 g/kg IBW as Brad's target with no CKD-specific reduction (only a 'consult your doctor' caveat).
items.suggested_fix: Reconcile the two: either state in the reference that the algorithm uses a lower 1.0 g/kg IBW target at eGFR < 45, or note the CKD reduction is not part of Brad's published target. The reference should not imply 1.2 g/kg IBW applies unchanged to CKD.

items.quote_a: | Osteoarthritis pain | 10-12 g/day | 6+ months | Collagen hydrolysate | Bruyere 2012 [23], Kumar 2014 [24] |
items.quote_b: | Joint pain (osteoarthritis) | Hydrolyzed collagen peptides | 5-10 g | 3-6 months |
items.summary: The osteoarthritis collagen hydrolysate dose range differs between the two excerpts (10-12 g/day vs 5-10 g/day), and the minimum duration differs (6+ months vs 3-6 months).
items.suggested_fix: Align the osteoarthritis dose and duration ranges across the two files, using the trial data both cite. Excerpt B itself notes that the benefit appeared at 6 months but not at 3 months in one trial.

items.quote_a: | Skin hydration/elasticity | 3-5 g/day | 12 weeks | Collagen peptides | Choi 2014 [33] |
items.quote_b: | Skin hydration/elasticity | Hydrolyzed collagen peptides | 0.5-10 g (range used in trials) | 12 weeks or more for elasticity |
items.summary: The skin hydration/elasticity dose is given as 3-5 g/day in A but as a range of 0.5-10 g across trials in B.
items.suggested_fix: State that the trials used a wider range (0.5-10 g/day) rather than implying 3-5 g/day is the studied range, or make clear A is describing a single trial.

items.quote_a: Hypercalcemia (serum calcium more than 10.5 mg/dL) is rare in healthy people and usually results from cancer, primary hyperparathyroidism or other conditions [1].
items.quote_b: Toxicity causes hypercalcemia (serum calcium > 11.1 mg/dL) with serum 25(OH)D typically above 150 ng/mL [1].
items.summary: The two pages define hypercalcemia with different serum calcium cutoffs (10.5 mg/dL vs 11.1 mg/dL).
items.suggested_fix: Align the two pages on a single serum calcium threshold for hypercalcemia, or state explicitly that the 11.1 mg/dL figure is a toxicity-level threshold rather than the definition of hypercalcemia.

items.quote_a: Calcium citrate and acetate reduce levothyroxine absorption about as much as carbonate [102].
items.quote_b: Iron reduces the absorption of levothyroxine (do not take it within 4 hours of iron), levodopa, ciprofloxacin (take it 2 hours before or 6 hours after iron) and tetracyclines such as doxycycline.
items.summary: The calcium excerpt's note that calcium citrate and acetate reduce levothyroxine absorption about as much as carbonate sits oddly with its own '4 hours apart from calcium carbonate' spacing rule, and the claim has no counterpart in the iron excerpt; this is a weak, probably non-contradictory overlap.
items.suggested_fix: Consider stating the 4-hour levothyroxine separation for all calcium forms, not just carbonate, since the excerpt itself says citrate and acetate reduce absorption about as much.

items.quote_a: Calcium also interferes with tetracycline antibiotics, so separate them from calcium by 3 hours [104][121].
items.quote_b: Take tetracycline and quinolone antibiotics at least 2 hours before or 4 to 6 hours after magnesium, and bisphosphonates at least 2 hours apart from it [1]; ask your doctor or pharmacist how far apart to take the others.
items.summary: Tetracycline separation guidance differs between the two pages (3 hours for calcium vs 2 hours before or 4 to 6 hours after for magnesium).
items.suggested_fix: Harmonise the tetracycline separation windows, or state that they are mineral-specific, so a reader taking both minerals gets one workable schedule.

items.quote_a: take dolutegravir or ciprofloxacin 2 hours before or 6 hours after calcium [1][120]
items.quote_b: Take tetracycline and quinolone antibiotics at least 2 hours before or 4 to 6 hours after magnesium, and bisphosphonates at least 2 hours apart from it [1]
items.summary: Ciprofloxacin (a quinolone) is given a 6-hour post-dose gap for calcium but a 4 to 6 hour gap for magnesium.
items.suggested_fix: Align the post-dose interval for quinolones across the two pages, or note that the ranges differ by mineral.

items.quote_a: In trials lasting 4 to 12 weeks, oral glutathione was well tolerated, though two people in one trial had a temporary rise in liver enzymes [61][80].
items.quote_b: In 566 military recruits, adverse events were about as common on NAC as on placebo (27.4% and 26.7%) [80], and two schizophrenia trials found no difference in side effects between NAC and placebo [29][81].
items.summary: The two pages cite the same reference number [80] for different studies (a 12-week glutathione trial in women versus a 566-recruit NAC trial), and [81] for both a nitroglycerin/NAC trial and a schizophrenia trial, so the reference lists conflict.
items.suggested_fix: Reconcile the reference numbering between the two pages so each number points to a single source.

items.quote_a: The glycine dose is close to the 3 g studied in clinical trials, and the 2,400 mg counts the glycine carried by the magnesium bisglycinate chelate.
items.quote_b: **General supplementation (to fill dietary gaps):** Brad includes 126 mg in his own supplements, about 30% of the RDA, as a top-up to a healthy diet, not a replacement for it [45].
items.summary: A says the 2,400 mg glycine in Sleep by Dr Brad includes the glycine from the magnesium bisglycinate, whereas B's elemental magnesium figure is in a product that A describes as having glycine as a separate ingredient (the glycine counts are inconsistent about whether the bisglycinate glycine is separate from the 2,400 mg).
items.suggested_fix: Clarify in one file whether the 2,400 mg glycine figure includes or excludes the glycine carried by the bisglycinate, so the two product descriptions agree.

items.quote_a: In a small pilot trial in older adults, it corrected glutathione deficiency [11].
items.quote_b: A placebo-controlled human study found that GlyNAC corrected glutathione deficiency in older adults and improved hand grip strength (Brad's current guidance, 31 Jul 2026).
items.summary: The GlyNAC trial in older adults is described as an open-label pilot of 8 people in A and in B's overview, but as a placebo-controlled study of 36 participants in B's 'Current view' section.
items.suggested_fix: Reconcile B's 'Current view' description with the pilot trial it describes elsewhere (open-label, 8 older adults, 24 weeks). If a separate placebo-controlled study was meant, cite it distinctly so readers do not conflate the two.

items.quote_a: Iron reduces the absorption of levothyroxine (do not take it within 4 hours of iron), levodopa, ciprofloxacin (take it 2 hours before or 6 hours after iron) and tetracyclines such as doxycycline.
items.quote_b: Vitamin C may increase levothyroxine absorption (one trial gave 500 mg with each dose to people with gastritis), so if you take levothyroxine, talk to your prescriber before starting, stopping or changing vitamin C [155].
items.summary: Iron is said to reduce levothyroxine absorption while vitamin C is said to increase it, so the advice on combining these supplements with levothyroxine differs.
items.suggested_fix: Reconcile the levothyroxine guidance across the two pages, noting that the vitamin C effect rests on a single trial in people with gastritis. Say whether iron and vitamin C are meant to be taken together in people on levothyroxine.

items.quote_a: Iron reduces the absorption of levothyroxine (do not take it within 4 hours of iron), levodopa, ciprofloxacin (take it 2 hours before or 6 hours after iron) and tetracyclines such as doxycycline.
items.quote_b: Zinc might bind quinolone and tetracycline antibiotics in the gut, which could lower absorption of both; take the antibiotic at least 2 hours before or 4 to 6 hours after zinc (6 hours after for ciprofloxacin) [1][102].
items.summary: Both excerpts give a separation interval for ciprofloxacin, but the iron excerpt says 2 hours before or 6 hours after iron while the zinc excerpt gives a general quinolone window of 2 hours before or 4 to 6 hours after, so the guidance is not stated consistently.
items.suggested_fix: Check the ciprofloxacin timing against the cited sources and use one wording in both references. The two excerpts agree on 2 hours before and 6 hours after for ciprofloxacin specifically, so this may only need aligned phrasing.

items.quote_a: The UL for iron is **45 mg/day** for adults (ages 14+) and **40 mg/day** from birth to age 13 [2][6].
items.quote_b: Megadoses can harm. Adult upper limits include 4,000 IU of vitamin D, 45 mg of iron and 40 mg of zinc a day [60][76][63][81].
items.summary: Excerpt B's list of adult upper limits is consistent for iron (45 mg) but this is not a real conflict on closer reading; flagged only for human look because B's iron UL line omits the age 14+ scope.
items.suggested_fix: No change required if the adult scope is understood; optionally add 'ages 14+' for consistency with the iron reference.

items.quote_a: The FNB set no UL because of vitamin K's low potential for toxicity [78].
items.quote_b: Vitamin E inhibits platelet aggregation and antagonizes vitamin K-dependent clotting factors [1][2].
items.summary: This pair is borderline and probably not a true contradiction: A concerns vitamin K toxicity while B concerns vitamin E antagonizing clotting factors.
items.suggested_fix: No change is likely needed; both can be true. A human may want to confirm the two excerpts do not imply conflicting anticoagulant guidance.

items.quote_a: | Mild erectile dysfunction | Pure L-citrulline | 1.5 g/day (750 mg twice daily) | 1+ month | Based on Cormio et al. trial [49]; higher doses (up to 6 g/day) sometimes suggested |
items.quote_b: - **Erectile dysfunction:** 1.5 g per day showed benefit in mild ED [22]
items.summary: Both give 1.5 g/day citrulline for mild ED, but A says higher doses up to 6 g/day are sometimes suggested while B lists only 1.5 g/day. This is an omission rather than a clear contradiction, so it is probably not a real conflict.
items.suggested_fix: No change needed unless the knowledge base wants to align on whether higher doses are mentioned.

items.quote_a: | Erectile dysfunction (men) | 5 g/day | 4-6 weeks | 1.5 g/day is NOT effective |
items.quote_b: - **Erectile dysfunction:** 1.5-6 g per day; the 2022 RCT showing category improvement in ED severity used 6 g/day for 3 months [20][21]
items.summary: A states 1.5 g/day of arginine is not effective for erectile dysfunction, while B lists 1.5-6 g/day as the dose range used for ED.
items.suggested_fix: Align the ED dose range with the evidence that 1.5 g/day is ineffective, or reconcile the two sources (for example, note that the 1.5 g figure applies to citrulline, as B's own citrulline entry suggests).

items.quote_a: At very high doses (21-30 grams per day), nausea, vomiting, and diarrhea have been reported (Evans et al., *J Nutr Biochem*, 2004) [1].
items.quote_b: - **Upper range in studies:** Most gastrointestinal side effects occurred at single doses above 9 g, and they seemed to disappear when the daily amount was taken in divided doses [35]
items.summary: A puts the onset of GI side effects at 21-30 g/day, whereas B reports most GI side effects at single doses above 9 g, a much lower threshold.
items.suggested_fix: Reconcile the GI-effect threshold, noting the difference between total daily and single doses, since B says splitting doses prevented the effects.

items.quote_a: In a SELECT case-cohort analysis, vitamin E alone had no effect on prostate cancer risk in men with higher selenium status, but in men with lower selenium status it increased the risk of total (63%), low-grade (46%, not statistically significant), and high-grade (111%) prostate cancer [32].
items.quote_b: In men with lower selenium status, high-grade prostate cancer rose by 111% with vitamin E (Kristal, JNCI 2014) [31].
items.summary: Both pages report the same SELECT vitamin E and selenium-status result (111% rise in high-grade prostate cancer) but cite it to different reference numbers ([32] vs [31]).
items.suggested_fix: Check which reference number is correct for the Kristal 2014 case-cohort analysis and make the two pages cite it consistently.

items.quote_a: The AREDS tablet specifications (per daily dose of four tablets): 28,640 IU vitamin A (from beta-carotene), 452 mg vitamin C, 400 IU vitamin E, 69.6 mg elemental zinc (from zinc oxide), and 1.6 mg copper (from cupric oxide).
items.quote_b: In IU, 900 mcg RAE equals 3,000 IU of retinol or supplemental beta-carotene, and 700 mcg RAE equals about 2,333 IU [109].
items.summary: The lutein article expresses beta-carotene vitamin A as 28,640 IU (the older IU convention), whereas the vitamin A article treats supplemental beta-carotene at 1 mcg RAE = 3.33 IU, so the same IU figure is not equivalent across the two files.
items.suggested_fix: State that the 28,640 IU figure uses the older IU labelling for beta-carotene and give the RAE equivalent so it is not read against the RAE-based limits in the vitamin A article.

items.quote_a: If you are having chemotherapy or radiation, ask your oncologist before taking vitamin C [87].
items.quote_b: Oncologists generally advise against antioxidant supplements, including vitamin E, during chemotherapy or radiotherapy because they might reduce treatment effectiveness by protecting cancer cells from oxidative damage [2][73].
items.summary: Vitamin C is treated as an 'ask your oncologist' item during cancer treatment, while vitamin E (also an antioxidant) is described as something oncologists generally advise against, so the two files take different stances on antioxidant supplements during treatment.
items.suggested_fix: Align the cancer-treatment guidance across the two files, noting that vitamin C is also an antioxidant and that oncologists generally advise against antioxidant supplements during treatment, while keeping the 'ask your oncologist' advice.
